messages.subject: syntax for random number generation
parts:
I'm calling out an issue from the previous e-mail to make
sure Andrew sees it in time to give feedback.

Marcus makes a convincing case for only allowing
randomization in "transformed data" and "generated quantities".
With that, we can use the notation

x ~ normal(0,1);

to assign x to a random unit normal variate, instead of requiring

x <- normal_random(0,1);

Will the overload be confusing? In the model block,

x ~ normal(0,1);

translates to the C++

lp__ += normal_log(x,0,1);

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] syntax for random number generation
parts:
This sounds fine to me but I am still processing some of these ideas. Let me just ask some questions:

1. I'm trying to understand "<-" expressions, that is, expressions of the form a <- …
Is it corret that, in such expressions, the thing on the left of the "<-" can be an intermediate quantity (a "local variable" in the model) or a transformed perameter, but that's it? Thta is, you can't have data or parameters to the left of "<-"?

2. Would it be legal for a model to have multiple distribution calls for a parameter or for data? For example:
y ~ normal (0, 1)
y ~ normal (0, 2)
My guess, from my understanding of the model, is that the above two lines would be ok; they would just add two factors to the posterior density. Thats actually fine with me, I have no desire for Stan to forbid such specifications. I just want to check that I'm understandging things correctly.

3. I still find the "transformed paraameter" thing to be awkward but maybe that's the only way to do it. What is confusing me is that I see there being two reasons for defining transformed parameters: (a) simple post-processing. For example, we define theta[1] <- exp(phi[1])/(exp(phi[1])+exp(phi[2])+exp(phi[3])), etc.; (b) we want to save some intermediate quantities in the computation.

I bring up transformed parameters because I see something similar happening with generated quantities, for example in (manual) posterior predictive checks where we simulate y_rep. Given how Stan works, it's definitely important to define y_rep as a generated quantity rather than simply as another parameter in the model. But, as with transformed parameters, this is a computational thing. To a statistician, y_rep is just one more unknown quantity.

A

parts: Speaking as an outsider who muddled through figuring out how to use Stan, it may be a little confusing, but not insurmountable.  When I first looked at stan, the translation from ~ normal to <- normal_log was confusing for a bit. I tried "~ normal_log(..." at least once, and was confused that there was were only entries for "normal_log" rather than "normal" in the documentation. Admittedly, I skimmed the docs the first time.   Once I understood what was going on, the usage is consistent and now makes sense to me, something which I can't say about some parts of R.  I think that if in the documentation there was a big section on "~" and what it does in different contexts, this will work.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] syntax for random number generation
parts:
On 8/15/12 4:52 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> This sounds fine to me but I am still processing some of these ideas. Let me just ask some questions:
>
> 1. I'm trying to understand "<-" expressions, that is, expressions of the form a <- ï¿½

> Is it corret that, in such expressions, the thing on the left of the "<-" can be an intermediate quantity (a "local variable" in the model) or a transformed perameter, but that's it? Thta is, you can't have data or parameters to the left of "<-"?

The manual lays all of this out in gory detail.

On the left of an "<-" you can have any variable declared
in the block in which the "<-" shows up, including local
variables.

So you get transformed data vars on the left of <- in
the transformed data block, transformed parameter vars
on the left of <- in the transformed parameter block,
generated quantities on the left of <- in the generated
quantities block, and you can always have a local
variable (standard name, no scare quotes) on the left side
of <- in any statement block.

> 2. Would it be legal for a model to have multiple distribution calls for a parameter or for data? For example:
> y ~ normal (0, 1)
> y ~ normal (0, 2)
> My guess, from my understanding of the model, is that the above two lines would be ok; they would just add two factors to the posterior density. Thats actually fine with me, I have no desire for Stan to forbid such specifications. I just want to check that I'm understandging things correctly.

Yes, that's what happens. There's a to-do item to issue
a warning if a user does this, but I haven't coded it yet.
the problem is figuring out when it's really the same variable
if you have an expression for an index, as with

for (n in 1:2) y[n] ~ normal(0,1);
for (n in 3:4) y[n] ~ normal(0,1);

Here there's no conflict, but if you replace n with a more
complex expression, it gets hard to tell at compile time whether
you'll assign once or twice.

> 3. I still find the "transformed paraameter" thing to be awkward but maybe that's the only way to do it. What is confusing me is that I see there being two reasons for defining transformed parameters: (a) simple post-processing. For example, we define theta[1] <- exp(phi[1])/(exp(phi[1])+exp(phi[2])+exp(phi[3])), etc.; (b) we want to save some intermediate quantities in the computation.

> I bring up transformed parameters because I see something similar happening with generated quantities, for example in (manual) posterior predictive checks where we simulate y_rep. Given how Stan works, it's definitely important to define y_rep as a generated quantity rather than simply as another parameter in the model. But, as with transformed parameters, this is a computational thing. To a statistician, y_rep is just one more unknown quantity.

I'm open to alternatives, but this is the best I could
come up with.

They were designed for the following usage pattern, which
I tried to make clear in the manual:

+use in model, +print: transformed parameter
+use in model, -print: local variable
-use in model, +print: generated quantity

For a statistician, the key is +/- use in model.
Generated quantities, while they're just "one more
unknown quantity", by definition don't affect the joint
log probability over the parameters.

- Bob
